assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks combine laser cooling, magic-wavelength trapping and ultrastable lasers to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, two orders better than the caesium standard. This is the clearest case of the measurement-limited progress that matters most to me as a laser spectroscopist: a new instrument with a clean principle, many applications (redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants) and broad impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye's group took it to the highest accuracy and many-body-limited regimes. The two-person configuration is natural and clear. Others in the field (e.g. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Hall for the laser-stabilisation/comb background) are not in the credited names; the comb and cooling contributions are already recognised in earlier prizes (2005, 1997).
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (Japan, US, France, Germany, UK, China) confirm the clocks and compare them at 1e-18; the technique is mature, stable and long established, so recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Jun Ye also appears on other candidates, but a single laureate slot here is unambiguous.
Whether the committee prefers to treat clocks as an application of previously recognised cooling and comb work is a judgement; I do not regard it as disqualifying.
I have not independently verified the latest accuracy figures.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED translated cavity QED into superconducting circuits, giving strong coupling, dispersive readout and the architecture of present superconducting quantum processors. Originality is high and the lasting impact on quantum technology and quantum optics is large. It is also a fine example of coherent light-matter interaction engineered in a new platform.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al.) are the decisive papers; Girvin is a close fourth with a real claim, and the list cap of three forces a choice. I propose Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf as theory-plus-experiment representation, acknowledging Girvin's claim and Devoret's earlier circuit work.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many groups and a decade and a half of use. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which makes timing a delicate issue, but cQED is a distinct, mature discovery.
uncertainties: Attribution is genuinely contested between four named people and others (e.g. Devoret, Nakamura).
Overlap with the recent circuit-related prize may lead colleagues to wait.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices became a programmable quantum simulator of Hubbard physics: the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site-resolved microscopes and now studies of antiferromagnetism and dynamics. Impact on many-body physics and quantum simulation is large and the experimental control reflects atomic-physics craft that I know well.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Bruder, Cirac, Gardiner and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation (1998); Greiner, Mandel, Esslinger, Hansch and Bloch observed the Mott transition (2002); Bloch built the field and quantum gas microscopy. Cirac is credited and a legitimate alternative to Greiner; the three-name cap leaves a real allocation problem. Zoller-Bloch-Greiner is my choice, with Esslinger and Cirac as plausible alternatives not both available.
assessment.maturity: Mature and reproduced in dozens of groups; the simulator programme is still evolving but the foundational discoveries are well established. Quantum-gas physics has been recognised in 2001 (BEC), so this is a natural follow-on.
uncertainties: Credit is dispersed (Esslinger, Hansch, Jaksch, Cirac, Gardiner) and the credited-name list cannot capture it all.
Whether simulation results have yet produced decisive new physics is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy by detecting a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos beyond 100 TeV and by associating neutrinos with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane. This is a decisive instrument-driven discovery that created a field, in the tradition of earlier neutrino-detector prizes.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the kilometre-scale ice detector and the science case; Karle was central to the construction and detector development. Yoshida is credited but I regard the two-person configuration as the strongest, though the collaboration of several hundred and leadership roles (e.g. spokespersons, other design leaders) leave some attribution ambiguity.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux confirmed with several channels and by independent analyses; the 2018 blazar association is about 3 sigma and still developing, while the 2023 Galactic-plane result is newer. Core discovery is solid and recognition timely.
uncertainties: Individual attribution within a large collaboration is difficult.
Source identification remains partial; the diffuse-flux discovery should be the cited achievement.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into precision metrology of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and underpins proposed gravitational-wave and dark-matter detectors. This sits close to my sense of measurement accuracy as the limit of knowledge, and builds on laser cooling and coherent manipulation.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of atom-light interferometry, Pritchard's early demonstrations with gratings and light, and Kasevich and Chu's atom-fountain gravimeters give a plausible trio; Chu has a Nobel already, and others such as Chu's collaborators, Rasel, Cronin, Ketterle in precursors are not credited. The credit is quite diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Technique is mature and independently reproduced; commercial and field-deployed gravimeters exist. Fundamental-physics reach (equivalence-principle tests) is still being pursued, so some significance is prospective.
uncertainties: Diffuse attribution and overlap with the 1997 cooling and 1989 Ramsey-method prizes.
Whether the discovery is a single breakthrough or a long evolution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire lasers and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) made reliable femtosecond sources routine, enabling frequency combs, attosecond science, multiphoton microscopy and ultrafast spectroscopy. The tool-enabling impact is enormous, a bit like earlier laser-technology prizes (2018, 2023 benefitted from it).
assessment.attribution: Moulton demonstrated the Ti:sapphire gain medium; Sibbett's group reported Kerr-lens mode locking (with Spence and Sibbett); Keller invented the SESAM. Which of these is decisive is debatable and the three names do not fully capture Kerr-lens work (e.g. Spence, Kean), so allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature with decades of independent use; recognition has arguably been delayed, and the prizes of 2005 and 2023 relied on this technology.
uncertainties: Credit for Kerr-lens mode locking is contested and some contributors are outside the supplied names.
Instrument development of this kind may be ranked below fundamental discovery by some members.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres created solid-state quantum sensing, nanoscale NMR and room-temperature spin qubits and quantum registers. Related to my own work on coherent optical interaction in solid-state crystals; the discovery has broad technical and biological relevance.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group demonstrated single-NV optical detection and spin readout (1997) and Jelezko the coherent control and nuclear-spin registers; Lukin is credited for later quantum-network work and sensing proposals, but I believe the earlier two are the decisive pair for the specific discovery, while recognising others (Awschalom, Hanson, Budker) are not in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced across labs and in several applications; the field is still moving fast and some applications (biological sensing) are not yet fully mature, but the core discovery is stable.
uncertainties: Broad field with many possible contributors who are not credited.
Whether the committee sees the sensing impact as sufficiently fundamental.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and E91) connects quantum foundations with a concrete cryptographic task and has been demonstrated in fibre and from space. The conceptual originality is high and it complements the 2022 entanglement prize.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) are very clearly the originators; Ekert (E91) is a genuine independent proposal and a natural third. The three-name configuration is relatively clean.
assessment.maturity: Concept long established and demonstrated by many groups; practical deployment is limited by rate and distance, and the 2022 prize touched adjacent ground, which may weigh on timing.
uncertainties: Impact is largely future-oriented relative to the discovery.
Overlap with experiments recognised in 2022 may reduce urgency.
